tagline: A steep woodland descent joins a colonial road through preserved farmland
intro: Breakneck Hill Road descends steeply through the Moshassuck River Valley, winding among rock outcrops and mixed hardwoods before meeting Great Road’s gentler grade. The designated stretch follows Route 123 for 1.4 miles through Lincoln. Its stewardship plan identifies woodland, agricultural views and historic properties as the qualities behind the state’s approval of Lincoln’s request for scenic designation in 1993. Rhode Island’s transportation department also points to open fields and a towering sycamore among the route’s visible features.

Great Road was laid out in 1683 to connect Providence with Mendon, then a central Massachusetts trading center, linking valley settlements to Providence’s port. The Louisquisset Pike and Blackstone Canal later displaced it as a major transportation link. Great Road remained a local route and was not widened and paved until 1926. A further reconstruction of Breakneck Hill Road was completed in 2002.

Start at Route 146 and descend Breakneck Hill Road, with Lincoln Woods State Park along the south side. At the Great Road junction, Butterfly Pond and Butterfly Mill come into view. Continue along Great Road past Hearthside and Chase Farm to Manchester Print Works Road, the designated eastern endpoint. The Arnold House lies just beyond the scenic highway boundary.

moments.title: Hearthside
moments.text: Hearthside’s fieldstone walls enclose ten fireplaces, or hearths. Stephen Hopkins Smith built the Federal-style house at the meeting of Great Road and Breakneck Hill Road. Smith allegedly financed the house with Louisiana lottery winnings to woo a Providence woman, but the attempt failed. He also owned the nearby Butterfly Mill. The house became a model copied during the early twentieth-century Colonial Revival. It remained a private residence until Lincoln bought it in 1996, when the nonprofit Friends of Hearthside became its overseers. The house entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1973.

moments.title: Chase Farm
moments.text: Chase Farm’s open land preserves part of Lincoln’s agricultural landscape. A large dairy operation in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, it remained one of the town’s last working farms until 1965. Lincoln bought it in 1979 to preserve that heritage. The adjacent Hannaway Blacksmith Shop began as a carriage house and was converted by William Hannaway in 1901. The shop closed in the 1920s as automobiles replaced horses as the principal means of transportation. Along the road, stone walls, deciduous trees and fences mark the historic farm properties.

moments.title: Eleazer Arnold House
moments.text: The Eleazer Arnold House is a stone-ender, a building type brought from western England and used most commonly in northern Rhode Island. Its exposed fieldstone end walls contrast with wooden side walls. Preserved Whipple Arnold donated the house in 1919 to the organization now called Historic New England. Norman Isham led the first stabilization work in 1920; the house and chimney received further structural rehabilitation in 1950. A 1950 restoration removed later alterations to recover its seventeenth-century appearance. That appearance includes newer work: the leaded-glass windows, front door and door surround are twentieth-century replacements.
moments.notice: The stone end walls and wooden side walls show the construction that gives a stone-ender its name.
